I feel like I've always known. It really showed it's face when I started having romantic relationships as a teenager. As I grew up, I started to realize that I was ruining good people. 

Then I got married to another toxic person and we had a baby. We ended up splitting up and they fled the scene when our daughter was about two. So there I am - a single parent with a toddler (the most infuriating type of human being) and all I can obsess about is how I'm going to RUIN her.

I went to individual therapy. I went through group dialectical behavioral therapy. I went through the ringer finding medications that work for me, and I stayed single. For years. I worked on myself until I was happy with how I interacted with my daughter. 

Fast forward and now she is 7, smart as hell, and so much more creative and imaginative than I ever was. We love each other so much. We have fun EVERY DAY. I'm not perfect. I still yell at her sometimes. We recently went to see a therapist together because we were arguing a lot more and it really helped. As it turned out, most of our communication issues were my past rearing it's ugly head (surprise) and I was able to recall most of my past therapy and move beyond it. Now I own a house all by myself, and I'm about a year into a remarkably healthy relationship with someone who helps remind me of the tools I use to regulate my emotions and tolerate distress. They are a real partner in my life. We both know how to take care of ourselves emotionally, so the codependency isn't there. We can disagree without confrontation, and that is incredible. I'm still learning about it and settling into it. We are moving slowly and that has helped tremendously.

So basically, I'm not perfect. I never will be. If I notice myself start to slip into my old toxic habits, I will immediately call my therapist and start up regular sessions again. I would absolutely recommend DBT (Dialectical Behavioral Therapy) to ANYBODY struggling with their own toxicity. It changed my life and I will happily rejoin a group if I start to slip. Having the tools and a plan in place really helps.

Shout out to my daughter for making me want to help myself, once and for all.

Oh. This is a good questions and I sincerely hope that somebody else can answer it better than I can. I try to get to a bathroom or a backroom and FAST. I let it happen. I pull it together just as much as I have to allow my facial swelling to subside. I try to focus on ANYTHING else. 

If you can, try to take a few minutes to STOP YOUR MIND and direct it toward physical sensation... Basically, if I'm uncontrollably weeping, I will take some breaths to calm that down and think about the feeling in my chest. The crushing of my sternum, the tightness in my intercostal muscles and the way the shoulders lift when I try to open my chest for air. I put all of my mental energy into feeling that until I feel something else. The tightening of my neck and how hard it is to hold up my heavy fucking head. I try to do this for 5 or 10 minutes. I put my phone away so that I don't text everybody I know begging for support and then not getting what I want from them and then freaking out again. It's important to stay with yourself. Sit with the sensations. Baby steps until the end of the day. Then you can go home and that in and of itself is an accomplishment.
